summary: This informational RFC describes the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015 block cipher known as Kuznyechik, which has a 128-bit block length and a 256-bit key length. It is one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms.

eli5.summary: A block cipher scrambles messages in chunks using a secret key. Kuznyechik is a scrambling method from Russia, and this document explains how it works.

questions: how does kuznyechik key schedule work
subtitle: The Russian GOST block cipher with 128-bit blocks and 256-bit keys, written up for the Internet community.

tldr.problem: The Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015 defines a block cipher, and the Internet community needed an accessible description of it.
tldr.mechanism: Kuznyechik runs 128-bit blocks through ten round keys derived from a 256-bit key. Nine rounds apply XOR, a byte substitution and a linear transformation, and the last step is a final XOR.
tldr.outcome: The RFC restates the standard's definitions, parameters, key schedule, and encryption and decryption, with test examples. It is informational only.

today: RFC 7801 is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Scope and Background
sections.content:
RFC 7801 is a source of information about the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015. It describes a block cipher with a block length of n=128 bits and a key length of k=256 bits, called Kuznyechik. It is one of the set of Russian cryptographic standard algorithms, the GOST algorithms.

The standard covers basic block ciphers for confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of information in transmission, processing and storage. The algorithms are designed for hardware and software, and put no restrictions on the confidentiality level of the protected information.

The RFC says the cipher was developed by the Center for Information Protection and Special Communications of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation with participation of InfoTeCS JSC. The standard was approved by Decree #749 of the Federal Agency on Technical Regulating and Metrology on June 19, 2015.
sections.eli5: This is a write-up of an official Russian rulebook for a scrambling method. It scrambles data in blocks, using a secret key.

sections.title: Building Blocks of the Cipher
sections.content:
The cipher is built from a few transformations on 128-bit strings. X[k] XORs the block with a 128-bit key k. S replaces each of the 16 bytes using a fixed substitution called Pi, a nonlinear bijection on bytes whose 256 values are listed in the RFC. S^(-1) uses the inverse substitution.

R shifts the 16 bytes by one position and puts a new byte in front. That byte is computed by a linear function l over all 16 bytes, using addition and multiplication in the finite field defined by p(x)=x^8+x^7+x^6+x+1. L is R applied 16 times. F[k] is a step built from these pieces that the key schedule uses.
sections.eli5: The cipher mixes a block in three ways: adding a key, swapping every byte using a lookup table, and smearing the bytes together. Each of these can be undone, so the message can be unscrambled.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The key schedule turns the 256-bit key K into ten 128-bit round keys K_1 to K_10. K_1 is the left (high) half of the key and K_2 is the right half.

The remaining keys come from four repetitions of eight F steps. Each step uses a round constant C_i = L(Vec_128(i)), for i from 1 to 32. Each group of eight steps produces the next pair of round keys.
sections.eli5: One long secret key is stretched into ten shorter keys, one for each stage of scrambling.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
Encryption of a 128-bit block a applies LSX[K_1] through LSX[K_9] in turn. Each of those does an XOR with the round key, then S, then L. The result goes through a final X[K_10].

Decryption undoes this using the same round keys in reverse order. It applies X[K_10] first, then for each of K_9 down to K_2 it applies L^(-1), S^(-1) and an XOR, and ends with X[K_1].

The RFC describes only the basic block cipher. It does not describe modes of operation, although it cites ISO/IEC 10116 for the terms used.
sections.eli5: To scramble, you repeat add key, swap bytes, smear, nine times, then add a last key. To unscramble, you do the same steps backwards with the keys in the opposite order.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 5 is informative and not a normative part of the standard. It gives intermediate values for the transformations S, R and L, a full key schedule from a sample key, a test encryption and a test decryption.

For the test key 8899aabbccddeeff0011223344556677fedcba98765432100123456789abcdef, the plaintext 1122334455667700ffeeddccbbaa9988 encrypts to 7f679d90bebc24305a468d42b9d4edcd. Decrypting that ciphertext returns the original plaintext.
sections.eli5: The RFC includes a worked example with real numbers. If your own code gets the same answer, you probably built it right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is one sentence: "This entire document is about security considerations." It contains no further analysis, and the Scope section says only that the algorithms comply with modern cryptographic requirements.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about keeping secrets safe, so it has nothing extra to add in its safety section.
